az_kennel_wall.blurb: Kennel Wall is a small sport crag on the downhill side of the Windy Point cluster along the Catalina Highway, up in the Santa Catalina Mountains above Tucson at around 6,300 feet. Nine bolted lines, mostly short, run from about 5.6 to low 5.11, and six of them sit in the 5.10 range, so it suits climbers who are comfortable on moderate sport. The routes face east, which brings the sun in early. To reach the base, go to the neighboring Lobo Wall and pass around its side. The Windy Point overlook lot is the usual place to leave the car.

az_lobo_wall.blurb: Lobo Wall is a compact wall of about 50 feet at the Windy Point cluster on the Catalina Highway, in the Santa Catalina Mountains near Tucson. It holds nine routes, six sport and three trad, running from 5.8 to 5.12 with most in the 5.10 band. Two cracks and a chimney split the middle of the cliff, and the base is flat. The wall catches shade in the morning, and because the lines are short it works as a warm-up while you wait for other crags to cool off. A single rack of trad gear opens up a few extra options. Parking is the Windy Point overlook lot.

az_i_long_ryders_wall.blurb: Long Ryders Wall is a bouldering wall at the far east end of the Drysdale Trail, in the Lake Mary area near Flagstaff at roughly 7,000 feet. Nine problems range from V1 up to a single V7, with most falling between V2 and V4. The face bulges and is peppered with deep pockets, crimps and finger buckets, giving steep, powerful moves. It gets plenty of sun, so cool days in the 25 to 40 degree range are the ones to aim for. Reach it by following the trail east past the Booze Pig Wall and the Half-life Wall.

az_another_roadside_attraction_area.blurb: Another Roadside Attraction Area is a small cluster of nine boulder problems in the Groom Creek bouldering zone south of Prescott, around 6,000 feet. The boulders sit right above Senators Highway, across from the school bus pullout, so the walk is minimal. Difficulty is mostly easy: five problems are around V0, a couple more land in V1 to V2, and the headline line is a V4 with a sit start that goes to V6. The first boulder you meet is a loaf-shaped block with a wedge-shaped rock below it, and the others lie up and to the right of it. A handy warm-up stop near the road.
az_another_roadside_attraction_area.approach: The boulders sit just above the road, a very short walk up from the school bus pullout on Senators Highway.

az_stormwatch_wall.blurb: Stormwatch Wall is a small cliff in Northern Devils Canyon, part of the Queen Creek Canyon complex in central Arizona at about 4,200 feet. Of its nine routes, eight are bolted and one is trad, running from 5.6 to 5.11. Four sit in the 5.10 range, which makes it a good stop for a mid-grade day. The cliff is made up of volcanic cracks, spires and broken faces, and much of the climbing is on pocketed faces. Expect a hike in from the parking near the power substation, with an overlook that gives a view across the canyon to the wall.

az_dog_town.blurb: Dog Town is the northernmost of the four climbing areas in The Refuge, a valley in Lower Devils Canyon within the Queen Creek Canyon area of central Arizona. The main wall faces east and has two slightly detached buttresses beside it. Nine routes, mostly trad with two bolted lines, go from about 5.5 to 5.10, so the climbing is easy to moderate. The east exposure means morning sun and little shade later in the day, so it can run warm. The trail in is short, easy to follow and marked with cairns.
az_dog_town.approach: A short, easy walk on a path marked with cairns, leading from the dry creek bed to the foot of the wall.
